title: 2D Array - DS
directAnswer: You're given a fixed 6×6 grid and must return the maximum hourglass sum. An hourglass is the 7 cells in a 3×3 block minus the two middle-side cells. There are exactly 16 hourglass positions (top-left corner ranges over rows 0–3 and columns 0–3). Sum each one with a closed-form expression and track the max — no nested scanning of each block needed.

remember.pattern: Fixed-size mask slid over a bounded grid
rules: There are exactly **16** hourglasses in a 6×6 grid: 4 valid top rows × 4 valid left columns.
Initialize `best` to a **very negative** value, not `0` — sums can be negative when all 7 cells are negative.
The hourglass is **not** a full 3×3 block. The two middle-side cells `g[r+1][c]` and `g[r+1][c+2]` are excluded.
Iterate the top-left corner only over rows `0..3` and columns `0..3` so `r+2` and `c+2` stay in bounds.
Sum the 7 cells directly — there's no benefit to a prefix-sum here because the mask is tiny and fixed.
whenToUse: A fixed-shape stencil (hourglass, plus, cross) slides over a bounded grid
The grid dimensions are constant, so total work is a constant number of fixed-cost sums
You need the max/min of a small fixed pattern over every legal position
antiSignals: The window is a variable-size rectangle whose sum changes incrementally → 2D prefix sums
You need every subrectangle sum, not one fixed shape → integral image
The grid is huge and the mask is large → precompute partial sums instead of re-summing
remember.takeaway: When a fixed-shape mask slides over a bounded grid, the whole problem is 'enumerate every legal top-left corner, sum the masked cells, keep the best'. The only traps are the bounds (16 positions, not 36) and the negative-init for `best`.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can translate a visual shape into exact index offsets, get the loop bounds right so you never read out of bounds, and remember that an all-negative grid means `best` can't start at 0.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Initializing the running max to 0, which returns 0 on a grid where every hourglass sum is negative. Or looping the corner over 0..5 and indexing g[r+2] out of bounds.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say up front 'the corner ranges over a 4×4 region, so there are exactly 16 hourglasses, and the work is constant'. Name the excluded cells explicitly so the interviewer knows you read the shape, not a full 3×3.

problemStatement:
Given a 6×6 2D array `arr`, an *hourglass* is a subset of values with indices falling in this pattern within the array:

```
a b c
  d
e f g
```

There are **16** hourglasses in the array. Calculate the hourglass sum for every hourglass, then return the **maximum** hourglass sum.

An hourglass sum may be negative — at least one hourglass always exists.
understanding: The grid is fixed at 6×6. An hourglass is 7 specific cells: a full top row of 3, a single middle cell directly below the center, and a full bottom row of 3. Slide the top-left corner over the 4×4 region of valid corners, sum the 7 masked cells at each position, and report the largest sum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the grid always exactly 6×6?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes for the classic problem — that's why there are exactly 16 hourglasses. If it were n×n, the corner would range over (n−2)×(n−2) positions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can hourglass sums be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Values range from −9 to 9, so an all-negative hourglass is possible. Initialize the running max to a very negative number, not 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the hourglass the full 3×3 block?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. It excludes the two middle-side cells — only the center of the middle row is included. That's 7 cells, not 9.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need the location of the best hourglass or just the sum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the maximum sum for this problem.

examples.explanation: The hourglass with top-left at (3,2) is 2 4 4 / 2 / 1 2 4 = (2+4+4)+(2)+(1+2+4) = 19, the maximum.
Every hourglass is negative; the least-negative sum is −6. This is why you cannot start the max at 0.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Re-check Every Cell of Every 3×3 Block
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to show you understand why the smarter version isn't really needed here, then move on quickly.
hints: How many top-left corners give a valid 3×3 block inside a 6×6 grid? Count the rows and columns the corner can sit on.
For each block, you only need 7 of its 9 cells. Which two do you skip?
Add up the 7 cells, compare against the best so far, and remember to start the best at a negative value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The grid is fixed at 6×6, so there are a constant 16 hourglasses and each costs a constant 6 additions. Everything here is O(1) — the 'brute' label only means 'no precomputation'.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the top-left corner over every position where a full 3×3 block fits, then sum the 7 hourglass cells of that block directly.

**Why the corner stops at row 3 and column 3.** A 3×3 block anchored at `(r, c)` reads cells up to `(r+2, c+2)`. For those to stay inside a 6×6 grid you need `r+2 ≤ 5` and `c+2 ≤ 5`, i.e. `r ≤ 3` and `c ≤ 3`. So the corner ranges over a 4×4 region: 4 rows × 4 columns = 16 hourglasses. Run the corner to row 5 and you index `arr[7]`, which is out of bounds.

**Why we only touch 7 cells.** The hourglass excludes `arr[r+1][c]` and `arr[r+1][c+2]` — the left and right of the middle row. Only the center `arr[r+1][c+1]` survives. Reading all 9 and subtracting the two would also work, but it's clearer to sum exactly the 7 you want.

**Why `best` starts negative.** With values down to −9, an hourglass can sum as low as −63, and an entire grid can be negative. If you initialize `best = 0`, a fully-negative grid returns 0 — a sum that never actually occurs. Start at something like `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (Java) or `float('-inf')` (Python).
approaches.insight: On a fixed 6×6 grid this 'brute force' is already optimal — the work is a constant 16 hourglasses. The lesson isn't the algorithm; it's getting the loop bounds and the negative initialization right.

approaches.name: Constant Pass — Closed-Form Over 16 Hourglasses (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: This is the clean answer: state there are 16 fixed hourglasses, sum each with the closed-form mask, keep the max.
hints: Since the grid size is fixed, the number of hourglasses is fixed too. What's that number?
Each hourglass sum is the same expression with shifted indices — write it once, parameterized by the corner (r, c).
You never need to revisit a cell or store partial sums; one direct sum per corner is already constant total work.
approaches.complexityReasoning: 16 hourglasses × 6 additions = 96 additions regardless of input. Constant time, constant space.
approaches.explanation:
For a fixed-size grid the optimal solution *is* the direct enumeration — there's nothing asymptotically to improve. The value of treating it as 'optimal' is recognizing the structure so you write tight, correct code.

**The mask as a closed form.** Every hourglass sum is `top + mid + bottom` where `top = arr[r][c] + arr[r][c+1] + arr[r][c+2]`, `mid = arr[r+1][c+1]`, and `bottom = arr[r+2][c] + arr[r+2][c+1] + arr[r+2][c+2]`. Writing it as three named pieces makes the shape obvious and the off-by-one mistakes visible.

**Why no prefix sum helps.** A 2D prefix-sum array shines when you query many overlapping rectangles of varying size. Here the shape is fixed and tiny (7 cells), and there are only 16 queries, so building a prefix table costs more than it saves. Recognizing when *not* to add machinery is part of the answer.

**Generalizing to n×n.** If the grid were n×n, the corner would range over rows `0..n−3` and columns `0..n−3`, giving `(n−2)²` hourglasses and `O(n²)` total work. The 6×6 case is just `(6−2)² = 16`. Mentioning this generalization signals you understand the bounds rather than memorizing 16.
approaches.insight: The trade here is conceptual, not computational: name the three bands of the mask (top, center, bottom) so the index offsets are self-documenting. That single habit kills the off-by-one bugs that sink most attempts at this problem.

Forgetting the negative initialization — the most common wrong-answer cause.
Including the middle-side cells, turning the hourglass into a full block sum.

edgeCases.behavior: The length-based bounds (rows−2, cols−2) handle any n ≥ 3 with no code change.
Exactly one hourglass; the loops run once and return its sum.

commonMistakes: Initializing the running max to 0 instead of a very negative value.
Letting the corner loop run to index 5, indexing one or two rows/columns out of bounds.
Summing all 9 cells of the 3×3 block instead of the 7 hourglass cells.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Zero-initialized maximum
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a grid where every hourglass sum is negative, starting at 0 returns 0 — a value that no hourglass actually produces.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
// ... best = Math.max(best, sum);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Out-of-bounds corner range
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Running the corner over 0..5 makes arr[r+2] reach index 7 — an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Summing the full block
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adding arr[r+1][c] and arr[r+1][c+2] turns the hourglass into a 9-cell square and overcounts.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: s = sum(arr[r + dr][c + dc] for dr in range(3) for dc in range(3))

patternNote: Fixed-shape mask over a bounded grid. Enumerate every legal top-left corner, sum the masked cells, keep the best. The recurring traps are the bounds (count the valid corners) and the negative initialization. Generalizes to plus/cross stencils and to n×n grids.
